articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content_excerpt: United Auto Workers (UAW) President Shawn Fain and the union’s newly elected International Executive Board (IEB) were sworn into office for a new four-year term in a ceremony honoring the will of the membership and reaffirming the union’s commitment to fighting for its members and all working-class people. Press is encouraged to use photos from the swearing-in ceremony . The ceremony marked the beginning of a new term for Fain and the International Executive Board, who pledged to faithfully serve the union’s membership and advance the interests of UAW members, families, and their communities. UAW member and longtime union leader Paul Caucci administered the oath of office to Fain, who begins his second term as International Union president. articles.title: Economics News for Workers, October 2026
articles.content_excerpt: On September 16, the Federal Reserve Board raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percent, the first rate hike in three years. Minutes from the meeting which were released in early October indicate that the board of governors expects to impose another rate increase before the end of the year. They meet again on October 28 and December 9. The rate increase, while justified as a means to fight inflation, was primarily meant to reassure international financial markets that the U.S. will make good on its debt, which has spiraled due to the combination of tax cuts for the wealthy and military spending. articles.title: Dattner’s Architects Say They Want a Union
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content_excerpt: On the west side of Manhattan, near the entrance to the Holland Tunnel, there is a nearly seventy-foot-tall concrete building containing five thousand tons of road salt. The walls of the Spring Street Salt Shed slope inward and outward in enormous pale planes; the whole thing is meant to resemble a grain of salt. Across the street stands a much larger garage that accommodates more than 150 sanitation vehicles, its long facades covered in glass and aluminum louvers. The two buildings were designed together, an attempt to make a sprawling sanitation facility fit into a residential neighborhood where residents had initially fought its construction. articles.title: More Than Ball Fields
articles.author: Bill Gould
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For generations of Altadena families, Charles S. Farnsworth Park has been much more than ballfields at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains. It has been one of the places where Altadena comes together. Children learned to throw and catch there, parents watched from the stands, coaches became mentors and neighbors became friends. But Farnsworth has always served a broader community. Its playgrounds, tennis and pickleball courts and basketball courts provided recreation for all ages. articles.title: In India, “Cockroaches” Are Leading the Fight for Democracy
articles.author: Prajwal Bhat
articles.content_excerpt: On October 10, India’s capital city, New Delhi, was turned into a fortress as protesters tried to oppose a countrywide exercise to revise the electoral rolls. The protests were called by the Gen Z movement known as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), working with left-wing student groups, which forced the resignation of the minister of education in July. In response, the Indian government deployed more than twenty thousand police officers and paramilitary personnel, suspended internet access in central Delhi, and barricaded the city center. Thousands of protesters, including the leaders of the CJP and prominent opposition politicians, were detained. articles.author: Kevin Anderson
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Beginning in the marginalized banlieues, France’s high school revolt has become national in scope, taking on economic and racial oppression as well as police brutality. By October 13, the high school protest movement in France had mushroomed, prompting up to half a million people to take to the streets across the country. On that day, Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg made a solidarity visit to one of the high schools where it all started, Lycée Paul Eluard, in the impoverished Paris banlieue (suburb) of Saint-Denis. The Green Party has put the conversation back on track: the problem is not the lack of creative solutions to the Israeli occupation of Palestine. The problem is Zionism itself. To appreciate the significance of Motion A105, adopted by the Green Party of England and Wales on Oct. 4, consider its basic tenets. The party is now formally anti-Zionist. It endorses the Palestinian right of return, supports one democratic state throughout historic Palestine, reaffirms its commitment to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, distinguishes anti-Zionism from antisemitism, and calls for a full arms embargo against Israel. articles.title: Leftists Should Learn to Organize Like Evangelicals
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content_excerpt: If progressives and radicals had all read Rick Warren’s The Purpose Driven Church when it came out in 1995, we’d be far stronger today. It’s the most important book on organizing that most leftists haven’t read. Luckily, it’s not too late to discover it. Warren founded Saddleback Church in suburban Orange County in 1980, starting with a Bible study in his home. Fifteen years later, more than ten thousand people were attending its services each weekend, and Saddleback had planted twenty-six other churches. The Purpose Driven Church was Warren’s attempt to explain how he’d done it, so that other pastors could do the same. articles.title: Sweden’s Left Faces a Political Deadlock
articles.author: Rikard Warlenius
articles.content_excerpt: After four years of a right-wing government that the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) heavily influenced, the parties that refuse to cooperate with the SD secured a narrow victory in the general election on September 13. However, the winning side consists of four parties that are politically very far apart and have so far been unable to agree on a new government. While the Left Party refuses to support a government in which it does not hold cabinet posts, the neoliberal Center Party refuses to support a government that includes Left Party ministers. Nobody wants a snap election or a repeat of the extremely slow, 134-day process of forming a government that followed the 2018 election. But there is still no solution in sight to this stalemate. articles.title: UAW President Shawn Fain, Abdul El-Sayed in Candid Conversation on 2026 Midterm Stakes
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content_excerpt: Today, the UAW released an hour-long conversation between UAW President Shawn Fain and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Recorded the previous week at the UAW’s Solidarity House in Detroit, MI, the two Midwest-made trailblazers in their respective fields covered a wide range of topics — from faith and family to healthcare, retirement security, trade, AI and technology, and other important issues that matter to working-class voters ahead of Election Day. Michigan is one of several states where the UAW is running its most ambitious political operation in decades. articles.title: High School Protests Can Transform France’s Election Campaign
articles.author: Solange Manche
articles.content_excerpt: Since the outbreak of high school blockades and students protests in French Guiana and Mayotte this September , Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s party, La France Insoumise, has continued to rise in the polls. After a rally in Clermont-Ferrand last Sunday, filling the city’s biggest arena — the third-largest in France — Mélenchon was for the first time projected to make it to the runoff of the 2027 presidential election, in all possible scenarios lining up different candidates. Marine Le Pen, projected to win 35 percent of the vote in the first round, will almost certainly be his opponent in the final showdown for power. Republicans hope—and Democrats Fear—that the recent pattern of polls underestimating Republican (and Trump) support will save them this year. And there are certainly grounds to hope that. In 2016, most polls had Trump losing, but of course, he won. Polls overestimated Hillary Clinton’s support by 3 percent. In 2020, polls overestimated Democratic numbers by 4.7 percent (but they won anyway). In 2024, Democrats were overestimated by 2.9 percent, and of course Trump won a narrow victory (not the landslide he claims). The mid-term bias has been smaller. Unions are the only space in American society where socialist values of solidarity and “us vs. them” are openly spoken and encouraged, outside of DSA. It is about time for us to take back this space to fight for workers’ rights. Detroit DSA’s Jobs Fair on September 19th was as much about education as it was about encouraging folks to consider new job options. During the fair, about 60 participants heard from five different union members about why going to work within their fields can create legitimate change for the whole working class, while also improving their individual lives. articles.title: When Workers, Driving Customers or Saving Lives in the ER, Become Independent Contractors
articles.author: Boston DSA
articles.content_excerpt: [[{“value”:” By: Matt Wolfinger BOSTON – There’s a loophole in our labor laws spreading across the economy. From delivery drivers to nurses, corporations are classifying workers as independent contractors and using the promise of flexible work to cudgel labor rights. Nearly 12 million people in the United States, or seven percent of the workforce, describe independent contractor work as their primary source of income, according to the most recent data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Independent contractors aren’t protected under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), so they can’t unionize, aren’t entitled to benefits, a minimum wage, or overtime and can be fired at will.
